title: If Moses learned it, what was his fault?
source_text: τοῦτο γὰρ Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς Ἐπικουρείοις δοκεῖ. Τούτου οὖν, φησὶ, τοῦ λόγου τοῦ παρὰ τοῖς σοφοῖς ἔθνεσι καὶ ἐλλογίμοις ἀνδράσιν ἐπακηκοὼς ὄνομα δαιμόνιον ἔσχε Μωϋσῆς. καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο δὲ λεκτέον, ἵν᾿ αὐτῷ συγχωρηθῇ Μω(??)σέα ἀκηκοέναι ἀρχαιοτέρου λόγου καὶ τοῦτον Ἑβραίοις παραδεδωκέναι, ὅτι εἰ μὲν ψευδοῦς λόγου ἀκούσας καὶ μὴ σοφοῦ μηδὲ σεμνοῦ παρεδέξατο αὐτὸν καὶ παρέδωκε τοῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτὸν, ἔγκλητός ἐστιν· εἰ δ᾿, ὡς σὺ φῂς, συγκατέθετο δόγμασι σοφοῖς καὶ ἀληθέσι καὶ ἐπαίδευσε τοὺς οἰκείους δι᾿ αὐτῶν, τί κατηγορίας ἄξιον πεποίηκεν; ὡς εἴθε καὶ Ἐπίκουρος καὶ ὁ ἔλαττον αὐτοῦ εἰς τὴν πρόνοιαν ἀσεβῶν Ἀριστοτέλης καὶ οἱ σῶμα εἰπόντες τὸν θεὸν Στωϊκοὶ τοῦ λόγου τούτου ἤκουσαν· ἵνα μὴ πληρωθῇ ὁ κόσμος λόγου ἀθετοῦντος πρόνοιαν ἢ διακόπτοντος αὐτὴν ἢ ἀρχὴν φθαρτὴν εἰσάγοντος τὴν σωματικὴν, καθ᾿ ἣν καὶ ὁ θεὸς τοῖς Στωϊκοῖς ἐστι σῶμα, οὐκ αἰδουμένοις λέγειν αὐτὸν τρεπτὸν καὶ δι᾿ ὅλων ἀλλοιωτὸν καὶ μεταβλητὸν καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς δυνάμενον φθαρῆναι, εἰ ἔχει τὸν φθείροντα, εὐτυχοῦντα δὲ μὴ φθαρῆναι παρὰ τὸ μηδὲν εἶναι τὸ φθεῖρον αὐτόν. ἀλλ᾿ ὁ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν λόγος, ὁ τὸ ἄτρεπτον καὶ ἀναλλοίωτον τοῦ θεοῦ τηρῶν, ἀσεβὴς εἶναι νενόμισται, ἐπεὶ μὴ συνασεβεῖ τοῖς ἀσεβῆ περὶ θεοῦ φρονοῦσι λέγων ἐν ταῖς πρὸς τὸ θεῖον εὐχαῖς· „σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ.“ πεπίστευται δὲ καὶ ὁ θεὸς εἰρηκέναι τὸ „οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι.“
pass_a_gloss: For this seems [right] to Celsus and to the Epicureans. Having heard then, he says, this doctrine (λόγος) which is among the wise nations and notable (ἐλλόγιμος) men, Moses got a divine/daemonic name (ὄνομα δαιμόνιον). And to this it must be said, that it may be granted (συγχωρέω) him that Moses heard an older doctrine and handed it down (παραδίδωμι) to the Hebrews, that if, having heard a false (ψευδής) doctrine and not wise nor venerable (σεμνός), he accepted it and handed it down to those under him, he is blameworthy (ἔγκλητος); but if, as you say, he assented to wise and true dogmas and educated (παιδεύω) his own people (οἱ οἰκεῖοι) through them, what worthy of accusation (κατηγορία) has he done? Would that (εἴθε) both Epicurus and Aristotle, less impious (ἀσεβέω, ἔλαττον) than he toward providence (πρόνοια), and the Stoics who said God is a body (σῶμα), had heard this doctrine, so that the world would not be filled with a doctrine setting aside (ἀθετέω) providence or cutting it off (διακόπτω) or introducing a corruptible (φθαρτός) principle (ἀρχή), the bodily (σωματική), according to which God too is for the Stoics a body, they not being ashamed (αἰδέομαι) to say him changeable (τρεπτός) and through-all altered (ἀλλοιωτός) and transformable (μεταβλητός) and simply able to be destroyed (φθείρω), if he has one who destroys, but being fortunate (εὐτυχέω) not to be destroyed because nothing is the destroyer of him. But the doctrine of Jews and Christians, guarding (τηρέω) the unchangeable (ἄτρεπτον) and unalterable (ἀναλλοίωτον) of God, has been thought (νομίζω) impious (ἀσεβής), since it does not join in impiety (συνασεβέω) with those thinking impious things about God, saying in the prayers (εὐχή) to the divine (τὸ θεῖον): But you are the same (σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ). And God too is believed to have said: I have not been altered (οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι).
pass_b_english: For this is what Celsus and the Epicureans think. “Moses, then,” he says, “having heard of this doctrine, which was current among wise nations and men of renown, won a godlike reputation.” To this we must reply, even granting him that Moses heard an older doctrine and handed it on to the Hebrews: if he heard a false doctrine, one neither wise nor venerable, and accepted it and handed it on to those under him, he is open to blame; but if, as you say, he assented to wise and true doctrines and educated his own people by means of them, what has he done that deserves accusation?

Would that Epicurus too had heard this doctrine, and Aristotle, who is less impious than he toward providence, and the Stoics, who said that God is a body! Then the world would not have been filled with teaching that sets providence aside, or curtails it, or brings in a corruptible first principle, the bodily one, according to which God too is a body for the Stoics. They are not ashamed to say that he is changeable, alterable through and through, and mutable, and in short capable of perishing if he had anything to destroy him, but fortunate enough not to perish because there is nothing to destroy him. Yet the doctrine of Jews and Christians, which preserves the unchangeableness and unalterableness of God, has been thought impious, because it does not join in impiety with those who hold impious views about God, saying in its prayers to the Divine, “But you are the same” (Psalm 102:27); and it is believed that God also said, “I do not change” (Malachi 3:6).

choices.choice: Staged Greek shows '(??)' inside Μωϋσῆς and its cases (Μω(??)υσῆς, Μω(??)σέως): an encoding artefact for the diaeresis, no textual effect. The opening sentence ('τοῦτο γὰρ Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς Ἐπικουρείοις δοκεῖ') completes the last sentence of 1.20 (the view that Moses' words are empty myths admitting no allegory); the staged row puts it at the head of 1.21 and it is translated here. Celsus's sentence is direct speech with φησί, so it is quoted. 'ὄνομα δαιμόνιον ἔσχε' rendered 'won a godlike reputation': in Celsus's mouth δαιμόνιον is favourable (superhuman, divine), not 'demonic'; ὄνομα = repute. 'ἵν᾽ αὐτῷ συγχωρηθῇ' read as concessive ('even granting him'). 'διακόπτοντος' (cuts off/cuts short) refers to Aristotle's limitation of providence; rendered 'cuts it short'. 'εἰ ἔχει τὸν φθείροντα, εὐτυχοῦντα δὲ μὴ φθαρῆναι' rendered with English conditional 'if he had anything to destroy him' for natural sequence. Scripture: 'σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ' = LXX Psalm 101:28, which is Psalm 102:27 in English Bibles (102:28 in Hebrew); renumbered. 'οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι' = Malachi 3:6 (LXX ἐγὼ κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν καὶ οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι, 'I am the Lord your God and I do not change'); same numbering in LXX and English. Perfect 'οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι' (I have not been altered) rendered 'I do not change', its stative sense. 'τὸ θεῖον' rendered 'the Divine' (capitalised: the one true God addressed in prayer).
ὄνομα δαιμόνιον ἔσχε: 'won a godlike name' -> 'won a godlike reputation' (ὄνομα = repute; 'godlike name' read as if his name itself were godlike)
διακόπτοντος: 'cuts it short' -> 'curtails it' (Aristotle limits providence)
ἀλλοιωτὸν καὶ μεταβλητόν: 'altered and transformed through and through' (actual change) -> 'alterable through and through, and mutable' (-τος adjectives state capacity, matching τρεπτόν 'changeable')
Scripture checked: σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτὸς εἶ = LXX Psalm 101:28 = English Psalm 102:27 (renumbering correct); οὐκ ἠλλοίωμαι = Malachi 3:6 LXX (same numbering): both correct
